title: Stateless Node.js services: workers, shared state, and graceful shutdown
description: A Node process runs your JavaScript on a single event-loop thread, so using more cores and more machines means changing how the service is built. Each Question covers one piece: why instances must be stateless, `cluster` vs. `worker_threads`, moving sessions into Redis, what goes wrong with sticky sessions, draining connections on `SIGTERM`, liveness vs. readiness probes, and keeping CPU work off the event loop. The code and the libuv thread-pool details match current Node.

questions.title: Why do users get randomly logged out after scaling to three instances?
questions.description: A login service stores each user's session in a module-level `Map` in process memory. It works fine on one instance. Then the team adds a load balancer and runs **three** identical instances.

options.text: Each instance has its own in-memory session map, so when a request lands on a *different* instance, the session isn't there. The service isn't stateless
The load balancer corrupts session cookies when it forwards them to more than one backend
Three instances exceed Node's default concurrent-connection limit, which silently drops sessions
Horizontal scaling requires HTTP/2 connection coalescing, and the instances still use HTTP/1.1

questions.explanation:
Horizontal scaling means running *N* interchangeable instances behind a load balancer, where any instance can serve any request. That works only if each request carries what it needs or can fetch it from shared storage. Once a process keeps mutable state in memory, like this session map, the instances stop being interchangeable. Instance A created the session, the load balancer sends the next request to B, and B has never seen it, so the user appears logged out.

The fix is to make the process **stateless**. Move sessions into a shared store such as Redis that every instance reads, or put the state in a signed token (JWT) that the client holds. The other options are scaling myths. Load balancers forward cookies unchanged, Node has no connection cap that drops sessions, and the HTTP version has nothing to do with where session state lives.

questions.title: Which tool is the idiomatic way to move CPU-bound work off the event loop?
questions.description: An endpoint resizes uploaded images **synchronously** with a pure-JS library. Under load, unrelated endpoints slow down and time out too, even a trivial `/health` check. You want to keep the work in the same Node process without freezing everything else.

images.alt: Inside one Node process, a wide main-thread bar holds your JavaScript and the event loop, exactly one of each. Below it, four libuv pool threads handle fs, crypto, dns, and zlib but never run your own JavaScript. A note says a synchronous loop over 5e9 iterations holds the one thread that runs handlers, so every other request, /health included, waits behind it. Two cards compare the tools. cluster runs separate processes with separate memory that share one listening port and talk by message passing. worker_threads runs several threads in one process, each with its own event loop, and they can share memory through SharedArrayBuffer. A closing line notes that cluster defaults to round-robin on Linux, with the primary handing each accepted connection to a worker.
images.caption: CPU work belongs on a thread with its own event loop.

options.text: `worker_threads`, usually through a pool such as Piscina, so the CPU work runs on a separate thread and the main event loop stays responsive
Wrap the resize in `setTimeout(fn, 0)` so it runs "asynchronously" off the event loop
Raise `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` so libuv runs your JavaScript across more threads
Add more `cluster` workers, since `cluster` takes CPU-bound calls off the event loop

questions.explanation:
Your JavaScript runs on one event-loop thread, so a synchronous CPU-bound section blocks everything on that thread. That's why `/health` stalls even though it has nothing to do with images. To keep the work in the process without blocking, run it on a **`worker_threads`** thread. Each worker has its own V8 isolate and event loop. A pool like **Piscina** reuses workers and queues tasks for you.

Why the other options fail:
- `setTimeout(fn, 0)` only *defers* the function to a later tick. It still runs on the same thread and blocks it just as hard.
- `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` grows libuv's background pool. That pool runs C++ async work such as `fs`, `dns`, `crypto`, and `zlib`, and it *never runs your JavaScript*, so it can't help a CPU-bound JS function.
- `cluster` adds more event loops, one per process, which raises total capacity. A blocking call still freezes the worker it runs on. `cluster` scales the fleet, but it doesn't move work off a given loop.

questions.title: Which statements about `cluster` vs. `worker_threads` are true?
questions.description: Both let one Node app use more of the machine. They differ in what they share: memory, event loops, and a listening port. Select every **true** statement.

images.alt: Inside one Node process, a wide main-thread bar holds your JavaScript and the event loop, exactly one of each. Below it, four libuv pool threads handle fs, crypto, dns, and zlib but never run your own JavaScript. A note says a synchronous loop over 5e9 iterations holds the one thread that runs handlers, so every other request, /health included, waits behind it. Two cards compare the tools. cluster runs separate processes with separate memory that share one listening port and talk by message passing. worker_threads runs several threads in one process, each with its own event loop, and they can share memory through SharedArrayBuffer. A closing line notes that cluster defaults to round-robin on Linux, with the primary handing each accepted connection to a worker.
images.caption: Separate processes below, separate threads beside them.

options.text: `cluster` forks separate **processes**, each with its own memory and V8 instance, and they don't share memory
`worker_threads` run inside one process and can share raw memory through a `SharedArrayBuffer`
`cluster` is built to spread **network I/O across CPU cores** by running several event loops behind one shared port
Because they live in the same process, two `worker_threads` also share a single event loop
A variable you change in one `cluster` worker is instantly visible to the other workers

questions.explanation:
The two tools solve different problems.

`cluster` runs **multiple processes**. It forks copies of your app that share a listening port. Each copy has its own memory, V8 instance, and event loop, and the copies talk only through IPC messages. Nothing is shared by reference, so a change in one worker is invisible to the others. Use it to spread **I/O-bound** traffic across cores.

`worker_threads` runs **multiple threads in one process**. Each thread is its own V8 isolate with its **own event loop**. Because they share a process, threads can share raw bytes through `SharedArrayBuffer` and send structured-cloned messages over a `MessagePort`. Use it to offload **CPU-bound** work.

The two false options flip this model. Each worker thread has its *own* event loop, and `cluster` workers have *separate* memory, so no variable is shared between them.

questions.title: How does `cluster` distribute incoming TCP connections by default?
questions.description: You run the `cluster` module on Linux with 4 workers and the **default** configuration.

images.alt: Inside one Node process, a wide main-thread bar holds your JavaScript and the event loop, exactly one of each. Below it, four libuv pool threads handle fs, crypto, dns, and zlib but never run your own JavaScript. A note says a synchronous loop over 5e9 iterations holds the one thread that runs handlers, so every other request, /health included, waits behind it. Two cards compare the tools. cluster runs separate processes with separate memory that share one listening port and talk by message passing. worker_threads runs several threads in one process, each with its own event loop, and they can share memory through SharedArrayBuffer. A closing line notes that cluster defaults to round-robin on Linux, with the primary handing each accepted connection to a worker.
images.caption: The closing line shows the primary accepting a connection and handing it off.

options.text: The primary process owns the listening socket, accepts connections, and hands them to workers **round-robin** (`SCHED_RR`)
Every connection goes to the worker with the lowest process id
The kernel assigns each connection to a random worker, with no coordination
Each connection is broadcast to all workers, and whichever calls `accept()` first wins it

questions.explanation:
On every platform **except Windows**, `cluster.schedulingPolicy` defaults to **`SCHED_RR`**, round-robin. The primary process is the only one listening on the port, and it deals accepted connections to workers in turn. Node made round-robin the default because it spreads load evenly.

The alternative, **`SCHED_NONE`**, is the default on Windows and is closest to the option where workers race to `accept()`. The primary shares the listening socket and lets the OS pick which worker's `accept()` wins. In practice the OS tends to favor a few workers, so load piles up unevenly, which is the problem round-robin fixes. You can switch policies with `cluster.schedulingPolicy` or the `NODE_CLUSTER_SCHED_POLICY` environment variable.

questions.title: Where should the shared session state live?
questions.description: The team has decided the login service must be stateless. Now sessions need to be visible to **all three** instances and survive restarts and deploys.

options.text: In a shared external store such as **Redis**, so every instance reads and writes the same data
In each instance's memory, replicated to the other instances over HTTP every so often
In each instance's memory, with every user pinned to one instance so their session is always reachable
In a local file on each instance's own disk

questions.explanation:
A stateless service still has state. The **process** just doesn't hold any. Shared, mutable state moves to a **backing service** that every instance talks to, most often **Redis**. It's fast, every instance can reach it, and per-key TTLs let sessions expire on their own. Any instance can now serve any request, because the data lives outside the process. A signed token held by the client is the other stateless option.

Each wrong option brings per-instance state back. Replicating over HTTP is racy, only eventually consistent, and still loses data on restart. Pinning users to an instance is **sticky sessions**, which brings back affinity and state. A local file is still per-instance and temporary, because instance B can't read instance A's disk and a redeploy wipes it.

questions.title: Which of these are real drawbacks of sticky sessions?
questions.description: With sticky sessions, also called session affinity, the load balancer sends a client back to the same instance on every request. Select **all** that apply.

options.text: A deploy or crash of that instance wipes the in-memory sessions of every client pinned to it
Load can become uneven, with long-lived clients piling onto a few instances while new ones sit idle
They let you keep mutable session state in process memory, so the service never becomes stateless
They make autoscaling smoother, because every new instance immediately gets a fair share of *existing* traffic
The HTTP specification requires sticky sessions for any service behind a load balancer

questions.explanation:
Sticky sessions are a workaround for keeping state in the process. Binding each client to one instance costs you what you scaled out for. If the instance goes down, its sessions go with it. Affinity concentrates traffic, so load gets uneven. And a new instance only attracts *new* clients, so it can't relieve existing hotspots. Sticky sessions also remove the pressure to move state out of the process, so the coupling stays.

The Twelve-Factor App is blunt about it:

> Sticky sessions are a violation of twelve-factor and should never be used or relied upon. Session state data is a good candidate for a datastore that offers time-expiration, such as Memcached or Redis.

The two false options get it backwards. New instances do *not* take over pinned traffic, and no spec requires sticky sessions.

questions.title: What should a Node process do on `SIGTERM` to shut down gracefully?

images.alt: Five numbered steps run from SIGTERM to exit. First, SIGTERM arrives. It isn't SIGINT, and it isn't SIGKILL, which can't be handled. Second, fail the readiness probe so the Service drops the Pod from its endpoints and new traffic stops. Third, call server.close() to stop accepting connections while in-flight requests finish. Fourth, highlighted, close the idle keep-alive sockets, because server.close() waits for every socket and an idle keep-alive socket never ends. Fifth, release database pools and queues and exit 0 inside the grace period. Two cards contrast the probes. When a liveness probe fails, the kubelet kills and restarts the container. When a readiness probe fails, the Pod keeps running but leaves the Service's endpoint list.
images.caption: The whole sequence, in the order that produces zero failed requests.

options.text: Stop accepting new connections with `server.close()`, let in-flight requests finish, release resources, then call `process.exit(0)`
Call `process.exit(0)` immediately so the orchestrator can start a replacement sooner
Ignore `SIGTERM` and let the `SIGKILL` that follows tear the process down
Throw an uncaught exception so the stack unwinds and closes sockets on the way out

questions.explanation:
`SIGTERM` asks the process to stop. You have until the grace period ends, 30 seconds by default in Kubernetes, before `SIGKILL` ends the process no matter what. The graceful pattern is the snippet above. **`server.close()`** stops accepting *new* connections and lets active requests finish. Its callback fires once every connection has closed, and then you free resources and exit.

The other options are how deploys start returning errors:
- `process.exit(0)` right away cuts off every in-flight request mid-response, and clients see resets or 502s.
- Ignoring `SIGTERM` just waits for `SIGKILL`, which **can't be caught** and gives you no chance to drain.
- Throwing an exception crashes the process with no ordered cleanup.

questions.title: Why does `server.close()` hang even with no requests in flight?
questions.description: A service handles `SIGTERM` by calling `server.close()` and exiting in its callback. In production, though, the process often hangs until the orchestrator force-kills it, even when no requests are in progress.

images.alt: Five numbered steps run from SIGTERM to exit. First, SIGTERM arrives. It isn't SIGINT, and it isn't SIGKILL, which can't be handled. Second, fail the readiness probe so the Service drops the Pod from its endpoints and new traffic stops. Third, call server.close() to stop accepting connections while in-flight requests finish. Fourth, highlighted, close the idle keep-alive sockets, because server.close() waits for every socket and an idle keep-alive socket never ends. Fifth, release database pools and queues and exit 0 inside the grace period. Two cards contrast the probes. When a liveness probe fails, the kubelet kills and restarts the container. When a readiness probe fails, the Pod keeps running but leaves the Service's endpoint list.
images.caption: Step 4: idle keep-alive sockets keep `server.close()` waiting.

options.text: Idle HTTP **keep-alive** connections stay open, and `server.close()` waits for *every* existing connection to end before it calls back
`server.close()` only works on HTTPS servers, and a plain HTTP server needs `server.destroy()` instead
Node refuses to exit while any `setInterval` timer exists, whatever the connection state
The callback passed to `server.close()` never runs unless you call `server.unref()` first

questions.title: How do failing liveness and readiness probes differ in Kubernetes?
questions.description: Both probes check the same container, but the kubelet reacts differently when each one fails. Focus on that difference in *behavior*.

images.alt: Five numbered steps run from SIGTERM to exit. First, SIGTERM arrives. It isn't SIGINT, and it isn't SIGKILL, which can't be handled. Second, fail the readiness probe so the Service drops the Pod from its endpoints and new traffic stops. Third, call server.close() to stop accepting connections while in-flight requests finish. Fourth, highlighted, close the idle keep-alive sockets, because server.close() waits for every socket and an idle keep-alive socket never ends. Fifth, release database pools and queues and exit 0 inside the grace period. Two cards contrast the probes. When a liveness probe fails, the kubelet kills and restarts the container. When a readiness probe fails, the Pod keeps running but leaves the Service's endpoint list.
images.caption: One probe restarts the container. The other only takes it out of traffic.

options.text: A failing liveness probe makes the kubelet **restart** the container. A failing readiness probe removes the Pod from Service endpoints so it **stops getting traffic**, without a restart
A failing readiness probe restarts the container, and a failing liveness probe only logs a warning
Both probes restart the container, and the only difference is their default timeout
Liveness probes run only at startup, and readiness probes run only during shutdown

questions.explanation:
The two probes answer different questions.

A **liveness** probe asks whether the container is alive or stuck beyond recovery. If it fails, the kubelet **kills and restarts** the container.

A **readiness** probe asks whether the container can serve traffic right now. If it fails, Kubernetes **removes the Pod from the Service's endpoints**, so the load balancer stops sending it requests. The container keeps running and can recover.

This lets a process that's alive but busy, say warming a cache or waiting on a dependency, leave rotation without being killed. The option where a failing readiness probe restarts the container swaps the two, and restarting on every brief readiness failure would cause needless restart loops. A third probe, the **startup** probe, covers slow boots, which is why "liveness runs only at startup" is also wrong.

questions.title: What should a Pod do first when it receives `SIGTERM`?
questions.description: You want **zero** failed requests during a rolling deploy.

images.alt: Five numbered steps run from SIGTERM to exit. First, SIGTERM arrives. It isn't SIGINT, and it isn't SIGKILL, which can't be handled. Second, fail the readiness probe so the Service drops the Pod from its endpoints and new traffic stops. Third, call server.close() to stop accepting connections while in-flight requests finish. Fourth, highlighted, close the idle keep-alive sockets, because server.close() waits for every socket and an idle keep-alive socket never ends. Fifth, release database pools and queues and exit 0 inside the grace period. Two cards contrast the probes. When a liveness probe fails, the kubelet kills and restarts the container. When a readiness probe fails, the Pod keeps running but leaves the Service's endpoint list.
images.caption: Readiness comes before `server.close()`, not after.

options.text: Start failing its **readiness** probe, or wait briefly, so the load balancer stops sending new requests, *then* call `server.close()` to drain in-flight ones
Call `server.close()` immediately and keep passing readiness so traffic keeps arriving
Exit as fast as possible to keep the deploy window short
Fail the **liveness** probe so Kubernetes restarts the Pod cleanly

questions.explanation:
Pod termination has a race built in. When a Pod is deleted, Kubernetes **removes it from Service endpoints and sends `SIGTERM` at about the same time**. The endpoint removal reaches every kube-proxy and ingress *asynchronously*, so for a short window after `SIGTERM`, new connections can still arrive. If you call `server.close()` first, those connections hit a server that has stopped accepting and fail immediately.

The safe order is to stop being routable first and stop the server second. Flip readiness to NotReady, or just `sleep` a few seconds, so the endpoint removal takes effect. Then call `server.close()` to let existing requests finish. That's **connection draining**. Closing first gets the order backwards, exiting immediately drops in-flight work, and failing *liveness* triggers a restart instead of a drain.

questions.title: While one `/report` request runs, what happens to other requests?

images.alt: Inside one Node process, a wide main-thread bar holds your JavaScript and the event loop, exactly one of each. Below it, four libuv pool threads handle fs, crypto, dns, and zlib but never run your own JavaScript. A note says a synchronous loop over 5e9 iterations holds the one thread that runs handlers, so every other request, /health included, waits behind it. Two cards compare the tools. cluster runs separate processes with separate memory that share one listening port and talk by message passing. worker_threads runs several threads in one process, each with its own event loop, and they can share memory through SharedArrayBuffer. A closing line notes that cluster defaults to round-robin on Linux, with the primary handing each accepted connection to a worker.
images.caption: One main thread runs every handler, and a blocking loop holds it.

options.text: They all wait until the loop finishes, because the synchronous loop blocks the single event-loop thread
They run in parallel, because Node spawns a new thread for each incoming request
Only other `/report` requests are blocked, and requests to other routes are unaffected
libuv automatically moves the loop to its thread pool, so nothing is blocked

questions.explanation:
Node runs your JavaScript on **one** thread, driven by the event loop. A synchronous CPU-bound section never gives control back to the loop, so the loop can't run *any* other pending callback until it ends. Every concurrent request on *any* route waits in line, and even `setTimeout` callbacks fire late. The route doesn't matter, because the thread is busy.

This is the main reason to keep CPU work off the request path. Move it to `worker_threads` or a pool, push it onto a background **job queue**, or scale out with `cluster` so at least the *other* workers stay responsive. Node doesn't spawn a thread per request, and libuv's thread pool runs only certain async C++ tasks such as `fs`, `dns`, and `crypto`, never your synchronous JavaScript.

questions.title: How many threads does libuv's thread pool have by default?
questions.description: People say "Node is single-threaded," yet libuv keeps a small pool of background threads for work like `fs` and `crypto`. Assume `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` is unset.

images.alt: Inside one Node process, a wide main-thread bar holds your JavaScript and the event loop, exactly one of each. Below it, four libuv pool threads handle fs, crypto, dns, and zlib but never run your own JavaScript. A note says a synchronous loop over 5e9 iterations holds the one thread that runs handlers, so every other request, /health included, waits behind it. Two cards compare the tools. cluster runs separate processes with separate memory that share one listening port and talk by message passing. worker_threads runs several threads in one process, each with its own event loop, and they can share memory through SharedArrayBuffer. A closing line notes that cluster defaults to round-robin on Linux, with the primary handing each accepted connection to a worker.
images.caption: The pool row, drawn at its default size.

questions.explanation:
libuv's thread pool has **4** threads by default. You can change that with the `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` environment variable, up to 1024 in current Node. The pool backs APIs that have no native async OS primitive: file-system operations, `dns.lookup()`, parts of `crypto` such as `pbkdf2`, `scrypt`, and `randomBytes`, and `zlib`.

This number confuses people for two reasons:
1. **Network I/O doesn't use the pool.** The OS handles sockets through epoll, kqueue, or IOCP, so thousands of open connections don't use up the 4 threads.
2. **The pool never runs *your* JavaScript.** A bigger pool can't unblock a CPU-bound JS function. That's what `worker_threads` is for. Pool size matters only when many pool-backed tasks, like heavy `fs` or `crypto` work, run at once.

questions.title: Which signal asks a container to shut down gracefully?
questions.description: Kubernetes, `docker stop`, and most orchestrators stop a container by sending one specific POSIX signal first, waiting out a grace period, and only then sending `SIGKILL`. Type the signal's name, such as `SIGxxx`.

images.alt: Five numbered steps run from SIGTERM to exit. First, SIGTERM arrives. It isn't SIGINT, and it isn't SIGKILL, which can't be handled. Second, fail the readiness probe so the Service drops the Pod from its endpoints and new traffic stops. Third, call server.close() to stop accepting connections while in-flight requests finish. Fourth, highlighted, close the idle keep-alive sockets, because server.close() waits for every socket and an idle keep-alive socket never ends. Fifth, release database pools and queues and exit 0 inside the grace period. Two cards contrast the probes. When a liveness probe fails, the kubelet kills and restarts the container. When a readiness probe fails, the Pod keeps running but leaves the Service's endpoint list.
images.caption: Step 1, plus the one signal a process can't handle.

questions.explanation:
The graceful-stop signal is **`SIGTERM`**, signal number 15. `docker stop` and Kubernetes send it first and wait out a grace period. In Kubernetes that's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, **30s** by default. Then they send **`SIGKILL`**, signal 9, which **can't be caught, blocked, or ignored** and ends the process at once.

That's why graceful shutdown lives in a `process.on('SIGTERM', …)` handler. It's your one chance to stop accepting connections, drain in-flight requests, and release resources before the hard kill. `SIGINT` is what Ctrl-C sends in a terminal. It's handy in development, but orchestrators don't use it.
